papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. papers.title: DisCell: Separating Spillover from Niche Response in Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Molen, R., Toosi, H., Ferreira, P. F., Lagergren, J.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics at single-cell resolution measures every cell in its place in the tissue, but diffusion and segmentation errors also add transcripts of neighboring cells to a cell's counts. This spillover makes a cell resemble its neighbors, and a response to the niche makes cells in the same niche resemble each other. Both tie a cell's expression to its surroundings. The count data alone cannot tell the two apart. Findings from single-cell transcriptomes, such as a gene program that is higher in one niche than in another or signaling genes that change depending on the neighborhood, may therefore be artifacts of spillover. Current models describe a cell by its intrinsic state together with either its niche response or spillover, but none models all three. We present DisCell, the first method that models all three components jointly and measures how robust each finding is to spillover. DisCell is a generative model that describes single-cell gene expression profiles in terms of two latent variables, an intrinsic state and a response to the niche, and adds spillover from its neighbors as a separate term. DisCell fits the model at increasing levels of spillover and recomputes each finding on the spillover-free expression to see how much spillover it withstands. DisCell also estimates the most spillover a section can contain, and a finding that holds even at that amount is not explained by spillover. In simulated tissue, DisCell recovers each cell's intrinsic state and response and tells findings created by spillover apart from genuine responses. On five sections of ovarian and lung tissue, the intrinsic state keeps more of each cell's own properties, measured by its cell-cycle phase, than any competing method that holds as little of its neighborhood. Within each cell type, the model partitions the variation of each gene into intrinsic state, niche response and spillover. Using DisCell, we rank findings about niches by their robustness to spillover and confirm that a previously reported finding withstands spillover, that esophageal cancer cells in niches infiltrated by immune or stromal cells express more of an epithelial-mesenchymal transition program. DisCell also predicts what the gene expression of a cell type would be in another niche, with its spillover part separated, at lower error on most tasks than the competing method built for this purpose. Training the model takes under ten minutes on one consumer GPU for sections of up to 400,000 cells.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.

papers.title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics
authors: Qian, W., Song, Y., Welch, J. D.
papers.abstract: Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distinguish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.

Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omic profiling and spatial transcriptomics across anatomically and molecularly diverse MRTs, generating a comprehensive multimodal MRT dataset at single-cell resolution. We leveraged this resource to identify candidate tumor-specific dependencies, which were subsequently functionally validated in vitro and in vivo in matched patient-derived models. We identified recurrent transcriptional metaprograms conserved across patients and molecular subtypes, including a previously undescribed shared core rhabdoid program, as well as a metaprogram characterized by extracellular matrix interactions, and preferentially localized in tumor-stroma intermixed neighborhoods, supporting identification of niche conditioning cues. Mechanistically, we identified regulatory wiring driving these metaprograms, with the core shared rhabdoid programme coordinated by a circuit centred on TCF12, ZNF148 and CHD2. Importantly, MET expression in primary tumors correlated with response, supporting biomarker-guided patient stratification for immediate clinical translation. authors: R, R., Balamuhunthan, S., Raman, K.
papers.abstract: Enzyme function prediction is a long-standing problem in biology, and deep learning methods have recently become popular to improve performance on this task. Here we thoroughly examine an approach that generates reactions absent from the training data from the enzyme alone. Existing methods such as BLASTp or CLIPZyme cannot, by design, output reactions that are absent from their training data or were not supplied at inference. The closest prior model, RxnPred, reports high fingerprint-similarity scores on held-out enzymes, a less stringent criterion than exact recovery, but fails to recover the correct answer on unseen reactions. We present a structure-conditioned generative model that outputs a complete reaction, reactants and products, and evaluate it on EnzymeMap_x, a reaction-disjoint benchmark in which no test reaction appears in training, under exact, stereo-respecting scoring. On this benchmark, within 400 sampled candidates, the model generates the complete, correct reaction for 25.0% of the subset of test enzyme--reaction pairs whose reaction is a new combination of metabolites seen in training. Surprisingly, it also correctly generates a few reactions composed of metabolites it has not seen in training (1.6%), though their embeddings are present in the vocabulary. With a lower budget, re-ranking places the correct reaction first for 5.6% of pairs and in the top ten for 12.4%, when the reaction is assumed not to be already known (0.2% and 8.1% without that assumption) along with confidence scores. Assessed more leniently, the model produces at least one correct reaction known for the enzyme (usually memorised from training) for 71.2% of test pairs. Going further, without any retraining, a sequence-only model given the reactants as well as the enzyme produces the correct product set for 9.5% of pairs within five candidates, without re-ranking. papers.title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
papers.abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $θ$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.

papers.abstract: Data imbalance frequently occurs in QSAR modeling, yet most studies focus on classification tasks, and few address regression tasks, as it is challenging to determine which regions of the data are sparse or dense. In this study, we systematically compare various strategies across GCN and fingerprint-based machine learning models. To evaluate model performance more meaningfully, we partitioned the target region into several subregions based on both domain knowledge and data distribution. We focused on the region of greatest practical interest. Our results demonstrate that selecting models based on this interest-region metric leads to more reliable performance than using the total region metric. papers.title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
papers.abstract: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

papers.abstract: Somatic mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1) define major subtypes of adult diffuse gliomas and occur across a broad spectrum of cancers. papers.abstract: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.

papers.title: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines
papers.abstract: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.

papers.abstract: Identifying differentially expressed genes is fundamental to elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying complex diseases. However, in complex disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), the genes exhibiting dysregulated expression may vary among patient subsets, reflecting the heterogeneity of the underlying pathological processes. Consequently, pathogenic genes are profoundly dysregulated in only a subset of patients. Conventional differential expression tools, such as DESeq2 and edgeR, are primarily designed to detect population-level expression shifts and may have limited power to identify subgroup-specific dysregulation. To overcome this limitation, we developed TailEnrich, a novel computational method that discovers dysregulated genes within patient subsets. TailEnrich independently tests the extreme left (downregulated) or right (upregulated) tails of a gene's expression distribution for disease sample enrichment. We quantify this enrichment using a new metric, i.e. the PE (Percentage of Enriched disease samples) score. On simulated datasets, TailEnrich demonstrates markedly improved accuracy over DESeq2 and edgeR in identifying dysregulated genes specific to patient subsets. Applied to AD gene expression data, TailEnrich uncovers a distinct, biologically relevant set of genes within key pathological pathways that are missed by mean shift-based approaches. TailEnrich provides a novel method for identifying dysregulated genes, and readily extends to other omics data including genomic variants and proteomics to uncover pathogenic genes in complex diseases.

papers.abstract: Background: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is driven by mutant KRAS, and RAS inhibitors now extend survival in previously treated metastatic disease. Whether treatment shrinks a tumour or only halts its growth depends partly on whether cancer cells die or stop dividing, yet how untreated PDAC cells are balanced between these programmes is unknown. Aims: We aimed to characterise the balance between apoptosis-associated and arrest-associated transcriptional programmes in treatment-naive PDAC and to examine their relationships with tumour subtype, TGM2 expression, tissue organisation, survival and drug sensitivity. Methods and results: We scored 52,999 malignant cells from 18 untreated patients in the Hwang atlas using a transcriptional contrast between genes associated with apoptosis and genes associated with resistance to apoptosis or cell-cycle arrest. In every patient the contrast was shifted toward the arrest-associated side: using equality between the two sides as the dividing threshold, 86.3% of cells with an informative score fell on that side, although the proportion depends on the threshold chosen. The shift recurred in the independent Steele atlas (median 71.6% per sample, range 37.1% to 90.8%). In the discovery cohort, tumours with higher basal-like scores had fewer arrest-side cells, and TGM2 expression was modestly higher on the arrest-associated side in both cohorts. The contrast did not track cell-line drug sensitivity or survival in bulk tumours. Conclusion: Untreated PDAC cells show a reproducible transcriptional bias toward anti-apoptotic and cell-cycle-arrest programmes. Whether this bias predicts cellular responses to treatment remains to be tested.

papers.title: SDHB deficiency silences ABCB1 expression and confers therapeutic vulnerability across multiple cancer types
authors: Guo, Q., Zhen, A., Howitt, B. E., Annes, J. P.
papers.abstract: Succinate dehydrogenase B (SDHB)-deficient cancers, including pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), exhibit aggressive clinical behavior with limited treatment options. To identify novel therapeutic vulnerabilities, we performed high-throughput drug screening using co-cultured human SDHB-deficient and SDHB-reconstituted UOK269 human renal cell carcinoma cells with dual fluorescence labeling. Several compounds displaying preferential cytotoxicity toward SDHB-deficient cells were known substrates of the ATP-binding cassette B1 (ABCB1) transporter, also known as Multidrug Resistance Protein 1 (MDR1). Accordingly, SDHB-deficient cells demonstrated markedly reduced ABCB1 expression, a phenotype confirmed across human SDHB-deficient PPGL, RCC, and GIST samples, but absent in IDH- or FH-deficient tumors. Mechanistic investigation revealed that KDM4A histone demethylase is downregulated in SDHB-deficient tumors, and KDM4A loss (or inhibition) is sufficient to reduce ABCB1 expression, globally increase H3K9me3 levels, and sensitize cells to cytotoxic ABCB1 substrates. TCGA analysis confirmed correlated KDM4A-ABCB1 expression in SDHB-deficient cancers, with ABCB1 levels predicting drug sensitivity across cancer cell lines. Clinical analysis demonstrated that SDHB-mutant PPGL patients treated with vincristine-containing chemotherapy exhibited significantly longer progression-free survival compared to non-SDHB patients. These findings establish a novel metabolic-epigenetic pathway linking SDHB deficiency to ABCB1 silencing and provide rational basis for repurposing vincristine, and related ABCB1 substrate vinca alkaloids, across SDHB-deficient cancer types; offering an alternative precision treatment approach for these challenging malignancies.

papers.title: Diagnostic Value in Discarded Reads: Re-evaluating Multi-Mapping cfDNA Fragmentomics and GC Bias in Early-Stage Cancer.
authors: Kadali, N., UPPALURI, K. R., Challa, H. J., Vempati, K. K.
papers.abstract: Background. Low-coverage plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing is an inexpensive substrate for cancer detection. Standard pipelines discard fragments with low mapping quality, which originate mostly from repetitive DNA, although pericentromeric satellite repeats are frequently hypomethylated in cancer. We asked whether the fraction of multi-mapping cfDNA fragments differs between early-stage cancer and matched healthy controls, and how it compares with conventional fragmentomic features under strict control of technical factors. Methods. We analysed public plasma cfDNA whole-genome sequencing from 25 patients with stage I to III breast cancer and 25 healthy controls matched 1:1 for age, sex, smoking and alcohol use, each pair processed in the same library and sequencing batch, and from 8 early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cases with 8 matched controls. For every sample we computed the fraction of autosomal fragments with MAPQ < 30 and the share of these fragments located in centromeric and heterochromatic cytobands, and related them to stage, grade and copy-number deviation as proxies of tumour burden. Classifiers were evaluated by leave-one-pair-out cross-validation in breast cancer and, trained on breast cancer only, applied unchanged to HCC. Robustness to GC content and sequencing depth was tested by within-fold residualisation and by fragment-level GC weighting. Conventional fragmentomic features (fragment length, end motifs, copy number, DELFI-like profiles and window features at transcription start sites) were evaluated under four GC-handling analyses. Results. The multi-mapping fraction was higher in breast cancer than in matched controls (median 5.38 % vs 5.19 %; higher in 19/25 pairs; paired p = 0.0006; cross-validated AUC 0.81, 95 % CI 0.67 - 0.94), in stage I (9/10 pairs), stage II (7/10) and stage III (3/5) disease and in every sequencing batch. The excess was concentrated in centromeric and heterochromatic bands, whose share of multi-mapping fragments rose from 22.0 % to 23.4 % (19/25 pairs; p = 0.004). Both signals persisted after within-fold adjustment for GC content and/or depth (AUC 0.64 - 0.76 for the multi-mapping fraction, 0.71 - 0.76 for the heterochromatic share) and under fragment-level GC weighting (18/25 pairs; p = 0.003). The multi-mapping difference was largest in stage I and decreased with stage (Spearman {rho} = -0.42, p = 0.04), and neither feature was associated with grade or copy-number deviation. In public tissue methylomes, satellites were hypomethylated in breast tumours to a similar extent as other late-replicating DNA, but the bin-level association between tumour hypomethylation and the cfDNA excess was weak and was explained by GC content. In HCC, the pre-specified endpoint, the breast-trained multi-mapping model, was not met (AUC 0.73; 5/8 pairs; sign test p = 0.36). In an exploratory analysis that was not pre-specified, the heterochromatic share was higher in 7/8 HCC pairs (p = 0.016; locked AUC 0.86, 95 % CI 0.62 - 1.00); across all 33 pairs, including the discovery pairs, it was higher in the cancer case in 26 (post hoc sign test p = 0.0007). In contrast, conventional fragmentomic features reached AUC 0.71 (breast) and 0.77 (HCC) only without fragment-level GC control; they tracked the per-sample coverage GC dependence and fell to chance under each of three GC-controlled analyses, including one that preserves promoter-specific signal. Conclusions. Multi-mapping cfDNA fragments, which are routinely discarded, differed between early-stage breast cancer and batch-matched controls, largely independently of GC content and sequencing depth, with an excess in centromeric and heterochromatic DNA. The signal did not scale with stage, its biological origin is unproven, and a read-quality contribution cannot be excluded from fragment files. It is a candidate marker that requires confirmation in larger cohorts with raw reads and tumour-fraction estimates.

papers.title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
authors: Libiseller-Egger, J., Gotsmy, M., Guillen-Gosalbez, G., Zanghellini, J.
papers.abstract: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.
